Let $f(x)$ be the $2L$-periodic extension of a function $F(x)$ from $x\in [-L,L)$ to $x \in \mathbb R.$ 
Given that $L=2$ and $f(x) = \cosh{(x+1)}$, find the $4$th cosine and the $4$th sine coefficients.

decisions.question: e-21835

source.question: e-21835
source.value:
Recall that multiplying the argument of a function by $k \neq 0$ represents the horizontal stretching of the corresponding graph by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{k}.$

Now, let $s=\dfrac{\pi}{L}x.$ Then, since $f(x)$ has a period of $2L,$ the function

$$
g(s) = f\left(\dfrac{L}{\pi}s\right)
$$

must have a period of $2L \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{L} = 2\pi.$ 

The Fourier series of $g(s)$ is

$$
g(s) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_n\cos(ns)+b_n\sin(ns),
$$

where:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\,\text{d}s \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)\,\text{d}s,\,n\ge 1 \\ {b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(ns)\,\text{d}s,\,n\ge 1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $s=\dfrac{\pi}{L}x$ and using the fact that $g(s) = f\left(\dfrac{L}{\pi}s\right),$ we get the Fourier series of $f(x){:}$

$$
f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}
a_n\cos\bigg(\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x}\bigg)+
b_n\sin\bigg(\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x}\bigg)
$$

Therefore, $4$th cosine coefficient of $f(x)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{4} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4s)\,\text{d}s \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(\frac{L}{\pi }s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4s)\,\text{d}s \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(\frac{L}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}(\frac{\pi }{L}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, $4$th sine coefficient of $f(x)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{4} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4s)\,\text{d}s \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(\frac{L}{\pi }s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4s)\,\text{d}s \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(\frac{L}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}(\frac{\pi }{L}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $L=2$ and $f(x)=\cosh(x+1),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{4} & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{2}x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi x)\,\text{d}x, \\ {b}_{4} & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{2}x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

source.question: e-21836
source.value:
For the Fourier series of a $2L$-periodic function, the constant term is given by

$$
a_0=\frac{1}{L}\int_{-L}^{L} f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $L=2$ and $f(x)=3x^2-4x+1$ for $x \in [-2,2).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}(3{x}^{2}-4x+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}+x]}_{-2}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(({2}^{3}-2\cdot {2}^{2}+2)-((-2)^{3}-2\cdot (-2)^{2}+(-2))) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2-(-18)) \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

decisions.question: e-21837

source.question: e-21837
source.value:
For the Fourier series of a $2L$-periodic function, the cosine coefficients are given by

$$
a_n=\frac{1}{L}\int_{-L}^{L} f(x)\cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\right)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $L=2$ and $f(x)=-5x+4$ for $x \in [-2,2).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
a_3 = \dfrac{1}{2}\int_{-2}^{2} (-5x+4)\cos\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}x\right)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=-5x+4\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=-5 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}x)\, & ⇒\,v=\frac{2}{3\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}x)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{3} & =\frac{1}{2}(uv\,{|}_{-2}^{2}-{\int }_{-2}^{2}v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{2}{3\pi }{[(-5x+4)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}x)]}_{-2}^{2}-{\int }_{-2}^{2}\frac{2}{3\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}x)\cdot (-5)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{2}{3\pi }[(-5(2)+4)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi )-(-5(-2)+4)\operatorname{sin}⁡(-3\pi )]+\frac{10}{3\pi }{\int }_{-2}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}x)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{2}{3\pi }\cdot 0+\frac{10}{3\pi }\cdot (-\frac{2}{3\pi }){[\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}x)]}_{-2}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{20}{9{\pi }^{2}}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3\pi )]) \\  & =-\frac{10}{9{\pi }^{2}}(-1-(-1)) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$
